content: This guideline, titled Cervical Cancer Control: A Guide to Essential Practice (C4-GEP), is primarily designed for policymakers, health program managers, and professionals in the health sector who are responsible for selecting strategies to prevent cervical cancer at national, regional, and district levels across low-, middle-, and high-income countries. The development of these guidelines adhered to the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development, with detailed methods described in Chapter 2 of the document. A Guideline Development Group (GDG) was formed, comprising experts, clinicians, researchers in cervical cancer prevention and treatment, health program directors, and methodologists. Conflicts of interest were managed according to WHO regulations. An independent group of scientists from a WHO collaborating center conducted systematic reviews and produced evidence summaries using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. GRADE evidence profiles were created for nine treatment-related questions, and the evidence-to-recommendation tables are available online. The systematic reviews revealed a limited number of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized studies with comparison groups. Consequently, most treatment recommendations are based on pooled results from non-randomized studies involving single groups of women receiving treatment without independent comparison groups. This underscores the need for further research, including rigorous non-randomized studies comparing two treatment groups when RCTs are not feasible or ethical. The guideline provides seven specific recommendations. For women with histologically confirmed CIN 2+ (Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia grade 2 or higher), regardless of HIV status, the expert panel strongly recommends the use of cryotherapy over no treatment and cold knife conization (CKC) over no treatment. Conditional recommendations include the use of CKC over LEEP (Large Loop Excision of the Transformation Zone). The quality of evidence for each recommendation is graded as high, moderate, low, or very low based on GRADE criteria. Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is a premalignant lesion diagnosed histologically as CIN 1, CIN 2, or CIN 3. If untreated, CIN 2 or CIN 3 (collectively referred to as CIN 2+) can progress to cervical cancer. Approximately 1–2% of women are estimated to have CIN 2+ annually, with higher rates (10%) reported among HIV-positive women. Diagnosis of CIN 2+ is based on histological examination of cervical biopsy specimens, with treatment recommended for confirmed cases. Adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS) is a precursor lesion for cervical cancer, typically found in the transformation zone and often associated with CIN. AIS is diagnosed cytologically and can be treated. Three principal treatment options for CIN are available in lowand middle-income countries: cryotherapy, LEEP, and CKC. In 2006, WHO published a guide to assist clinicians and program managers in diagnosing and treating CIN to prevent and control cervical cancer. This guide, known as C4-GEP, provides background information on CIN, its diagnosis, and treatment options. In 2009, WHO committed to updating this guide to reflect new evidence on HPV vaccination, cervical cancer screening methods, and treatments for cervical precancer. The updated guideline builds upon the 2011 WHO recommendations for the use of cryotherapy to treat CIN. It provides recommendations for the use of cryotherapy, LEEP, and CKC for histologically confirmed CIN 2+ and AIS. The document also describes the WHO methodology used to develop these guidelines, based on the GRADE approach, and includes evidence profiles and evidence-to-recommendation tables. The GDG identified nine key questions to guide the evidence review for CIN and AIS treatment. These questions followed the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcomes) format and addressed the comparative effectiveness of cryotherapy, LEEP, and CKC versus no treatment or each other. The GDG also prioritized outcomes for decision-making, including residual/recurrent CIN 2+, major bleeding, maternal death, HPV-negative status, major infections, premature delivery, spontaneous abortion, pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, and minor bleeding. The evidence synthesis involved systematic reviews of studies comparing cryotherapy, LEEP, and CKC for CIN 2+ and AIS. Data on harms were collected from studies involving treatment at any CIN stage, as the GDG determined that treatment harms are unlikely to depend on CIN stage. Issues related to resource use and feasibility were summarized by the WHO Steering Group, GDG, and External Review Group (ERG). The evidence was presented in absolute effects, applying risk ratios to baseline risks, and subgroup analyses were conducted to assess treatment effects by HIV status and age. The results of the systematic reviews and meta-analyses are being prepared for publication and will be available through the WHO website. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach, and the evidence was presented in GRADE evidence profiles.
